title: India's Operation Amistad Wins Hearts in Earthquake-Shattered Venezuela
excerpt: Two IAF C-17 Globemasters, 41 medical personnel, and indigenous BHISHM cubes — India's disaster-relief machine reaches Latin America as the death toll crosses 2,600.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • India's Operation Amistad delivers humanitarian aid to earthquake-hit Venezuela, with over 2,600 fatalities reported.
  • Two C-17 Globemaster aircraft transported 35 tonnes of relief supplies and a 41-member medical team.
  • The Indian Army field hospital is now operational, providing critical medical support to local communities.
  • The earthquakes, measuring 7.2 and 7.5, caused extensive damage, leaving over 15,000 homeless.
  • India's disaster-relief efforts enhance its global reputation as a first responder in humanitarian crises.
Operation Amistad: A Lifeline for Venezuela

India has launched **Operation Amistad** — Spanish for friendship — to deliver humanitarian assistance and disaster relief to Venezuela, which was struck by devastating back-to-back earthquakes on June 24 that have now killed at least 2,645 people and left more than 15,000 homeless. Two Indian Air Force C-17 Globemaster III heavy-lift aircraft departed for Venezuela on June 26, transiting through Abidjan in Côte d'Ivoire, carrying 35 tonnes of relief equipment, a 41-member rescue contingent including nine medical officers, and two BHISHM Cubes — India's indigenous, rapidly deployable modular medical facilities designed for disaster and humanitarian response. ## A Field Hospital in the Rubble The contingent, drawn from the Indian Army, is equipped to provide emergency medical care, trauma management, and life-saving surgical support. External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar announced the operation on X, writing: "India is committed to supporting the government and people of Venezuela in this difficult time." The Ministry of External Affairs confirmed that the relief consignment included an Indian Army Field Hospital unit with HADR pallets, 30 tonnes of relief supplies, six tonnes of medicines and medical equipment, and two BHISHM Cube portable hospitals under India's Aarogya Maitri Project. The BHISHM Cube — Bharat Health Initiative for Sahyog, Hita and Maitri — is a self-contained, modular medical unit that can be airlifted into disaster zones and made operational within hours. Each cube contains operating theatres, diagnostic equipment, and enough supplies to treat hundreds of patients. The technology, developed indigenously, has been deployed in previous Indian relief operations. > **""India stands shoulder to shoulder with the government and the people of Venezuela during this difficult period," the MEA said in its statement."** By early July, the Indian Army field hospital was fully operational in Venezuela and receiving gratitude from local communities, with the MEA sharing footage of Venezuelans thanking Indian medical teams for their life-saving work. ## The Scale of the Catastrophe ![Field Hospital — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/8/8c/47th_CSH0216.JPG) The twin earthquakes — measuring 7.2 and 7.5 on the Richter scale — struck northern Venezuela within seconds of each other on the evening of June 24, devastating the coastal state of La Guaira and large parts of Caracas. Hundreds of buildings collapsed, trapping thousands under rubble. As of July 3, the official death toll stands at 2,645 with more than 12,000 wounded, according to Venezuela's information ministry. But the true scale may be far worse: citizen-led efforts to register the missing have collected nearly 50,000 names, and the World Health Organization has warned that Venezuela's healthcare system is under "significant strain," with at least three health centres critically damaged. The United Nations has procured 10,000 body bags in anticipation of more deaths. International rescue teams, including from the United States and several Latin American nations, have joined the response.
Impact of the Earthquakes

## India's Growing First-Responder Role Operation Amistad follows a pattern of increasingly ambitious Indian disaster-relief missions that have bolstered New Delhi's reputation as a global first responder. In 2025, **Operation Brahma** deployed 118 personnel and a 200-bed field hospital to Myanmar after a 7.7-magnitude earthquake, treating over 2,500 patients. Before that, **Operation Dost** sent relief to Turkey and Syria in 2023, and **Operation Maitri** aided Nepal after its devastating 2015 earthquake. The Venezuela deployment is notable for its geographic reach — the C-17s flew over 15,000 kilometres across the Atlantic — and for demonstrating India's willingness to project humanitarian power well beyond its traditional neighbourhood in South and Southeast Asia. Prime Minister Narendra Modi has framed these operations as expressions of India's civilisational values. "India stands shoulder to shoulder with the government and the people of Venezuela during this difficult period," the MEA said in its statement. ## What It Means for the Diaspora

For Indian Americans and NRIs worldwide, India's disaster-relief operations have become a source of national pride and a tangible marker of the country's rising global stature. Each deployment — from Kabul to Mandalay to now Caracas — reinforces the narrative of India as a responsible power capable of rapid, effective humanitarian response on any continent. The operation also underscores India's expanding strategic engagement with Latin America, a region home to a small but growing Indian diaspora and one where New Delhi has been steadily deepening diplomatic and commercial ties.
